## Abstract

Classical Digital Soil Mapping harmonises horizon observations via
equal-area quadratic splines [@Bishop1999; @Malone2009] — a purely
mathematical object disconnected from pedogenesis. The **Pillar 2** of
`edaphos` replaces that spline with two Physics-Informed Machine
Learning (PIML) [@Raissi2019; @Karniadakis2021; @Willcox2021pinns]
models of the soil depth profile: a parametric pedogenetic Ordinary
Differential Equation (ODE), solved in closed form and fitted through a
horizon-average observation operator, and a Neural ODE
[@Chen2018neuralode] trained
by back-propagation through a fixed-step Runge-Kutta integrator on
`torch` [@PichlerRtorch]. Both models are demonstrated on the
`aqp::sp4` reference pedons and a hierarchical covariate-conditioned
extension closes the loop with Pillar 5.

## 1. Pedogenetic ODE

Let \(y(z)\) denote a soil property (e.g. clay fraction, SOC) at depth
\(z\ge 0\). The one-dimensional kinetic model of translocation
[@Jenny1941; @Minasny2016] assumes a depth-dependent relaxation
towards a parent-material asymptote \(y_{\infty}\) with rate
\(\lambda(z)\):
\[
\frac{dy}{dz}\;=\;-\lambda(z)\,\bigl(y(z)-y_{\infty}\bigr),\qquad
\lambda(z)=\lambda_{0}\,e^{-\mu z}.
\tag{1}
\]
Parameters \((\lambda_{0},\mu,y_{\infty},y_{0})\) carry explicit
physical meaning: \(\lambda_{0}\) is the surface pedogenetic rate;
\(\mu\) controls how quickly that rate decays with depth; and \(y_{0}\)
is the surface intercept.

\(y_{\infty}\) needs care, because it is **not** the value the profile
reaches. Equation (1) is separable and its solution is
\[
y(z)=y_{\infty}+(y_{0}-y_{\infty})
      \exp\!\Bigl[-\tfrac{\lambda_{0}}{\mu}\bigl(1-e^{-\mu z}\bigr)\Bigr],
\tag{2}
\]
so, with \(\kappa=\lambda_{0}/\mu\),
\(y(\infty)=y_{\infty}+(y_{0}-y_{\infty})e^{-\kappa}\). Because the rate
\(\lambda(z)\) decays with depth, the profile traverses only a fraction
\(1-e^{-\kappa}\) of the \(y_{0}\to y_{\infty}\) gap and then stops.
\(y_{\infty}\) is an equilibrium coordinate of the differential equation;
the parent-material extrapolation is \(y(\infty)\), and the two can differ
in sign. The fit is carried out in the identified, positive coordinates
\((y_{0}, y(\infty), \kappa, \mu)\), with \(\lambda_{0}\) and
\(y_{\infty}\) recovered for reporting. The implementation
[`piml_profile_fit()`][piml_profile_fit] evaluates (2) directly — the
equation has a solution, so integrating it numerically is only slower and
less accurate — and minimises
\[
\mathcal{J}(\theta)\;=\;
\sum_{j}\bigl(\bar y(z_{j}^{\text{top}},z_{j}^{\text{bot}};\theta)-y_{j}\bigr)^{2}
\;+\;\eta\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|_{2}^{2},\tag{3}
\]
with Nelder--Mead from several starting points. Two details matter. The
forward operator \(\bar y\) is the model's **average over the horizon**
\([z^{\text{top}}_j, z^{\text{bot}}_j]\), by Gauss--Legendre quadrature on
(2), rather than a point evaluation at the mid-depth — a laboratory value
is a layer average, which is the same observation-operator issue the
equal-area spline literature addresses [@Bishop1999; @Malone2009]. And the
Tikhonov term is centred on the data-driven start \(\theta_0\): on log
coordinates an uncentred penalty shrinks every concentration toward 1, and
in earlier versions, applied to the raw \(y_\infty\), it scaled with the
square of the property's units and silently did part of the fitting.[^psn]

[^psn]: Physics is imposed by the *forward model itself* — the
optimiser cannot produce a profile that violates the exponential
approach to \(y_{\infty}\), irrespective of data. This is the
strong-PIML regime sensu [@Karniadakis2021].

## 2. Dataset — `aqp::sp4`

We use the ten reference pedons of `aqp::sp4` with horizon
concentrations of clay, sand, Ca, Mg, K, CEC and CF.

```{r setup-gate, echo=FALSE}
# knit_exit() stops knitting AFTER this chunk finishes, so the guard
# must be the last thing in a chunk of its own -- otherwise the code
# it protects still runs.
library(edaphos)
.torch_ok <- requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&
             isTRUE(tryCatch(torch::torch_is_installed(),
                             error = function(e) FALSE))
if (!requireNamespace("aqp", quietly = TRUE)) {
  knitr::knit_exit("Package `aqp` not installed — skipping vignette.")
}
```

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
data(sp4, package = "aqp")
sp4$depth <- (sp4$top + sp4$bottom) / 2
head(sp4[, c("id", "name", "top", "bottom", "depth", "clay", "K")])
unique(sp4$id)
```

## 3. Mono-pedon fit: clay translocation in `napa`

The `napa` pedon is a canonical argillic-horizon case: clay increases
with depth through illuviation then converges to a plateau in the
parent material. The ODE (1) captures that dynamics without prescribing
the sign of \(y_{\infty}-y_{0}\).

```{r single-fit}
napa <- subset(sp4, id == "napa")
napa[, c("name", "depth", "clay")]
fit_napa <- piml_profile_fit(
  depths = napa$depth,
  values = napa$clay
)
fit_napa
```

```{r predict-grid}
grid_z <- seq(0, max(napa$depth) + 10, by = 1)
pred_napa <- data.frame(depth = grid_z,
                         clay  = predict(fit_napa, grid_z))
```

```{r plot-single, eval=requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = pred_napa, aes(clay, depth),
            linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(data = napa, aes(clay, depth),
             size = 3, colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Clay (%)", y = "Depth (cm)",
       title = "Napa — pedogenetic ODE vs. observed horizons") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## 4. Multi-pedon diagnostics

Fitting the full `sp4` dataset recovers an interpretable table where
every row has a direct pedological meaning.

```{r group-fit}
fits <- piml_profile_fit_group(
  sp4, id = "id", depth = "depth", value = "clay"
)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(k) {
  p <- fits[[k]]$params
  data.frame(
    pedon   = k,
    lambda0  = signif(p$lambda0, 3),
    mu       = signif(p$mu,      3),
    kappa    = signif(p$kappa,   3),
    y0       = signif(p$y0,      3),
    # the value the profile reaches -- NOT y_inf, which is reported
    # alongside it to show how far apart the two can be
    y_attain = signif(edaphos:::.piml_asymptote(p), 3),
    y_inf    = signif(p$y_inf,   3),
    rmse     = signif(fits[[k]]$rmse, 3)
  )
}))
tab
```

Read this table with `y_attain` — the value the profile reaches — and not
`y_inf`. On `colusa` and `tehama` the two differ by orders of magnitude,
and both are absurd: those pedons have three or four horizons, all in the
top 42 cm, with clay still rising at the deepest one. There is simply no
information in them about where the argillic horizon levels off, so the
curve is fitted through the observations and then points off to nowhere.
`print()` flags exactly these two, reporting how far down the
\(y_0 \to y(\infty)\) journey the deepest horizon actually got:

```{r flagged}
vapply(fits, function(f) f$progress, numeric(1))
```

On neither flagged pedon does the four-parameter equation improve on a
two-parameter straight line (next section: 3.018 against 3.016, and 0.839
against 0.836), which is the right outcome — the model should not be
credited for a shape it did not determine.

## 5. Non-physical baselines

Two baselines bound the improvement claim: the mean predictor and the
linear-in-depth regression. A meaningful PIML gain should come from
the physical constraint, *not* from extra parameters.

```{r baseline}
baseline_rmse <- function(sub, target) {
  y <- sub[[target]]
  c(mean   = sqrt(mean((y - mean(y))^2)),
    linear = sqrt(mean(stats::residuals(
                     stats::lm(y ~ sub$depth))^2)))
}
bench <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(sp4, sp4$id), function(sub) {
  bl <- baseline_rmse(sub, "clay")
  data.frame(pedon = sub$id[1],
             piml  = fits[[sub$id[1]]]$rmse,
             mean_baseline = bl["mean"],
             linear_baseline = bl["linear"])
}))
bench
```

## 6. Neural ODE variant

For profiles where the mono-asymptotic prior is violated — illuviated
bulges, E horizons beneath A, buried paleosols — `edaphos` offers a
Neural ODE alternative [@Chen2018neuralode]:
\[
\frac{dy}{dz}=f_{\theta}(z,y),\qquad
f_{\theta}=\text{MLP}(z,y;\,\theta).
\tag{4}
\]
The forward map is a fixed-step RK4 integrator written directly in
`torch`, so training back-propagates the squared-error loss through
the whole trajectory:
\[
\mathcal{J}_{\text{NODE}}(\theta)
   \;=\;\sum_{j}\Bigl(
      \underbrace{\int_{0}^{z_{j}}f_{\theta}(z,y(z))\,dz
                  +y_{0}}_{\text{RK4 rollout}}
      \;-\;y_{j}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]

```{r neural-ode, eval=.torch_ok}
nn_fit <- piml_neural_ode_fit(
  depths  = napa$depth, values = napa$clay,
  hidden  = c(16L, 16L), epochs = 500L,
  seed    = 1L, verbose = FALSE
)
nn_fit
pred_nn <- data.frame(depth = grid_z,
                       clay  = predict(nn_fit, grid_z))
```

```{r plot-neural, eval=.torch_ok && requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = pred_napa, aes(clay, depth,
            colour = "Parametric ODE"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = pred_nn,   aes(clay, depth,
            colour = "Neural ODE"),     linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = napa, aes(clay, depth),
             size = 3, colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Parametric ODE" = "steelblue",
                                  "Neural ODE"    = "darkgreen")) +
  labs(x = "Clay (%)", y = "Depth (cm)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Napa — parametric vs. Neural ODE") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## 7. Pillar 2 × Pillar 5 — the physics gate

Given a PIML fit (parametric or neural), the helper
[`al_physics_gate_piml()`][al_physics_gate_piml] constructs a
rejection function: candidates whose predicted target falls outside the
envelope \([\min(y_{0},y_{\infty}),\,\max(y_{0},y_{\infty})]\) inflated
by a `safety_factor` are eliminated from the greedy Active-Learning
selection (see the Pillar 5 vignette).

```{r gate, eval=.torch_ok}
gate <- al_physics_gate_piml(fit_napa, safety_factor = 1.2)
cand_dummy <- data.frame(dummy = 1:4)
gate(cand_dummy, predicted_mean = c(10, 25, 200, -5))
```

A hierarchical extension ([`piml_hierarchical_fit()`][piml_hierarchical_fit])
jointly fits a covariate-conditioned Neural ODE across pedons,
delivering a **per-location** envelope that
[`al_physics_gate_piml_hierarchical()`][al_physics_gate_piml_hierarchical]
feeds back into Pillar 5.

## 8. Bayesian posterior over the ODE parameters

[`piml_profile_fit()`][piml_profile_fit] returns a single point
estimate. For any honest downstream use — propagating parametric
uncertainty into a SOC-stock prediction, tuning a Pillar 5
Active-Learning acquisition under correct epistemic variance,
reporting publishable parameter intervals — we need the **posterior**
\(p(\lambda_0, \mu, y_\infty, y_0 \mid \text{depths}, \text{values})\),
not just the MAP.

The function
[`piml_profile_fit_bayesian()`][piml_profile_fit_bayesian] returns
that posterior through two nested approximations:

1. **Laplace approximation** (default, O(ms) per pedon). Gaussian
   posterior whose mean is the MAP and whose covariance is the inverse
   observed Fisher information at the MAP [@Bishop2006PRML, §4.4].
   Accurate when the posterior is well-identified; every call
   pre-samples 2 000 draws from \(N(\text{MAP}, \Sigma)\) for
   predictive convenience.
2. **Adaptive random-walk Metropolis** [@Haario2001] (~seconds per
   pedon). Proposal covariance starts at the Laplace covariance,
   scaled by the Roberts–Gelman–Gilks optimal factor
   \((2.38)^2 / d\), and is updated online by Haario recursion after a
   warm-up period — so non-Gaussian or multimodal posteriors are
   captured faithfully where Laplace would paper over them.

```{r bayes-laplace, eval=TRUE}
library(edaphos)

depths <- c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100)
values <- c(25, 18, 12, 8, 6.5)

fit_bayes <- piml_profile_fit_bayesian(depths, values,
                                         method = "laplace", seed = 1L)
fit_bayes
```

```{r bayes-predictive, eval=TRUE}
predict(fit_bayes,
         newdepths         = c(10, 20, 40, 80),
         interval          = 0.95,
         include_obs_noise = TRUE,
         seed              = 1L)
```

`include_obs_noise = TRUE` adds Gaussian observation noise with the
MAP-estimated \(\sigma\) onto every predictive draw, so the returned
interval represents the predictive distribution of a *future
observation* rather than the uncertainty on the mean function alone.

For the Neural-ODE variant the variational analogue is a **deep
ensemble** [@Lakshminarayanan2017ensemble]: `K` independent networks
trained from different random seeds produce an empirical posterior
whose mean and variance approximate the Bayesian predictive posterior
[@Wilson2020bayesian].

```{r bayes-deep-ensemble, eval=.torch_ok}
ens <- piml_neural_ode_fit_ensemble(depths, values,
                                       K = 5L, epochs = 300L, seed = 1L)
predict(ens, newdepths = c(10, 20, 40, 80), interval = 0.9)
```

## 9. Discussion and roadmap

The parametric ODE is mono-asymptotic and therefore optimal for
properties that decay monotonically toward a parent-material value
(SOC, some nutrients) but suboptimal for bimodal profiles, which the
Neural ODE handles by construction. Three complementary directions
remain on the roadmap:

* **Mass-conservation soft constraints** — augment the Neural ODE loss
  with a term penalising deviations from an integrated mass balance
  [@Minasny2017].
* **Adjoint-method Neural ODE** — for pedons deeper than 2 m, the
  back-propagation graph becomes memory-bound; the adjoint method of
  [@Chen2018neuralode] eliminates that scaling.
* **Hierarchical Bayesian pooling** — extending
  [`piml_hierarchical_fit()`][piml_hierarchical_fit] to the posterior
  regime that
  [`piml_profile_fit_bayesian()`][piml_profile_fit_bayesian] already
  exposes for single pedons, with covariate-conditioned priors over
  \((\lambda_0, \mu, y_\infty, y_0)\).
